word:greek-nt:G0012.explanation: Abyssos means the abyss, an unfathomable depth.

word:greek-nt:G0085.explanation: This word means “be distressed” or “to be troubled,” describing a person experiencing serious inner anguish or emotional disturbance. It presents distress as a genuine burden rather than a light concern. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each in a different verse. Its uses include language for intense personal distress, so the surrounding passage is important for showing what caused the trouble and how the person responded. The word itself focuses on the condition of being deeply troubled.

word:greek-nt:G0166.explanation: Aionios means age-long, enduring, or eternal. It describes both eternal life and eternal fire.

word:greek-nt:G0250.explanation: Aloe means a fragrant aloe wood, prepared as powder.

word:greek-nt:G0269.explanation: This word means “peaceable”: it describes a person or conduct characterized by peace rather than conflict. It is an adjective, so it identifies a quality or manner rather than naming an action by itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 3:2. Its basic sense is a calm, non-conflicting disposition, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes.

word:greek-nt:G0328.explanation: Anazōnnymi means to gird up or brace up for active effort.

word:greek-nt:G0377.explanation: Anapiptō means to lie down or recline, especially at a dinner table.

word:greek-nt:G0575.explanation: Apo means from. It can also mean away from.

word:greek-nt:G0636.explanation: This word means “to sail away from” or “to set sail.” It describes leaving a place by ship or beginning a voyage. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, all in Acts, and each use concerns travel by sea. The word functions as an action word, focusing on the departure or beginning of a sea journey rather than on the destination or the wider events surrounding the voyage. Its exact force in any particular verse is understood from the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G0724.explanation: Harpagē means plundering or robbery—the taking of possessions from others.

word:greek-nt:G0751.explanation: Archippus is a personal name referring to a man named in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Colossians and once in Philemon. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the name itself identifies the person, while each passage supplies the further information about him.

word:greek-nt:G0849.explanation: This word means “with one’s own hand,” describing something done personally and directly rather than through someone else. It emphasizes the person’s own action or involvement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 27:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to personal, hands-on action instead of delegated or indirect activity.

word:greek-nt:G0870.explanation: Aphobos means fearlessly or without fear.

word:greek-nt:G0984.explanation: Blaptō means to hurt or injure.

word:greek-nt:G1015.explanation: Bounos means a hill or hillock.

word:greek-nt:G1082.explanation: Gennesaret is the name of a fertile district by the lake of Tiberias. It can also name that lake.

word:greek-nt:G1208.explanation: Deuteros means second, identifying what holds the second place in an order. It can also mark a second occurrence, as when the rooster crowed a second time.

word:greek-nt:G1257.explanation: Dialeipō means to cease or stop.

word:greek-nt:G1301.explanation: Diatēreō means to keep safe. It can also mean to hold fast, as when sayings are kept in the heart.

word:greek-nt:G1419.explanation: This word describes something hard to carry—burdensome, heavy, or “ponderous.” It points to a load that is difficult for someone to bear or manage, whether understood as physical weight or as a demanding burden. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Matthew 23:4 and Luke 11:46. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains something excessively difficult to carry or bear.

word:greek-nt:G1420.explanation: This word means “dysentery,” an illness affecting the intestines. It names a physical sickness rather than an action, command, or character quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 28:8. The word identifies the kind of illness involved, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the particular details of the case. Its central meaning remains the medical condition itself: dysentery.【p03:word:greek-nt:G1420:identity】【p03:word:greek-nt:G1420:occurrences】【p01:word:greek-nt:G1420:reference:0】

word:greek-nt:G1486.explanation: Eiōtha means to be accustomed or to have a custom.

word:greek-nt:G1697.explanation: Hemmor is a personal name rendered Hamor in English.

word:greek-nt:G1763.explanation: Eniautos means a year, a cycle of time.

word:greek-nt:G1837.explanation: Exēcheō means to sound out or ring out, clearly or loudly.

word:greek-nt:G1868.explanation: Epainos means praise or commendation. It can express approval for doing what is good.

word:greek-nt:G1921.explanation: Epiginōskō means to come to know by directing attention. It can describe recognizing a person, perceiving something, or finding out a fact.

word:greek-nt:G1954.explanation: This word means “remaining”—what is left after something has already been removed, completed, or passed. It points to what continues or is still available, rather than to the whole of something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 4:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning is the portion or time still left. It functions as a concise description of what remains after an earlier part has been accounted for.

word:greek-nt:G1983.explanation: Episkopeō means to exercise oversight and care. It is used for watching carefully over people and for willingly overseeing a flock.

word:greek-nt:G2133.explanation: Eunoia means good will or kindliness.

word:greek-nt:G2191.explanation: Echidna means a snake or viper.

word:greek-nt:G2335.explanation: Theōria means a sight or spectacle.

word:greek-nt:G2465.explanation: Isangelos means equal to or like the angels.

word:greek-nt:G2559.explanation: Kakoo means to treat someone badly. It can also mean to harm someone.

word:greek-nt:G2560.explanation: Kakōs means badly, evilly, or wrongly.

word:greek-nt:G2638.explanation: Katalambano means to seize or take hold of. It can also mean to overtake. It can also mean to perceive or comprehend.

word:greek-nt:G2762.explanation: Keraia means the smallest stroke or mark in writing, like a tiny pen stroke or tittle.

word:greek-nt:G2906.explanation: Kraugē means a shout, cry, or clamor.

word:greek-nt:G2999.explanation: Latreia means service rendered to God, or worship.

word:greek-nt:G3040.explanation: Limen means a harbor, port, or haven.

word:greek-nt:G3079.explanation: Lysias is a personal name, identifying someone called Lysias. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea, but a proper name used to identify a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts: Acts 23:26 and Acts 24:22. The name itself gives the person’s identification; the surrounding passage supplies the details about who he was and what he did.

word:greek-nt:G3105.explanation: Mainomai means to be raving mad. It can also describe speaking as a madman.

word:greek-nt:G3314.explanation: Mesēmbria means midday or noon. It can also mean the south, as a direction.

word:greek-nt:G3361.explanation: Mē means not. It can also mean lest, introducing something to be prevented or avoided.

word:greek-nt:G3426.explanation: Modios means a dry measure, nearly two English gallons.

word:greek-nt:G3552.explanation: This word means “be sick” or “to be unhealthy.” It describes a person whose condition is marked by illness or poor health, rather than expressing a healthy state. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:4. Its basic sense is physical or figurative weakness, while the surrounding verse determines how that condition is being applied. The word itself centers on being unwell or lacking health.

word:greek-nt:G3673.explanation: This word describes someone who practices the same trade or craft as another person. Its central meaning is “of the same trade,” identifying a shared occupation rather than merely a general similarity. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 18:3. The word therefore points specifically to a person connected with another through the work or craft they both practice.

word:greek-nt:G3729.explanation: Hormao means to rush or hasten on.

word:greek-nt:G3822.explanation: Palaioō means to make old or obsolete. It can also describe something becoming old, as a garment grows old.

word:greek-nt:G3927.explanation: Parepidēmos means a stranger or sojourner, someone residing in a foreign country. Scripture applies it to people described as strangers and pilgrims on earth.

word:greek-nt:G3978.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to go on foot” or “to walk,” describing movement made by walking. It names the act of traveling by foot rather than simply indicating arrival or departure. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 20:13. That reference identifies its sole occurrence, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the action functions in that sentence. Its central meaning remains straightforward: walking or proceeding on foot.

word:greek-nt:G4052.explanation: Perisseuein means to exceed what is ordinary or necessary or to abound.

word:greek-nt:G4126.explanation: Pleo means to sail, travel by sea, or voyage.

word:greek-nt:G4180.explanation: Polylogia means wordiness, or speaking many words.

word:greek-nt:G4229.explanation: Pragma means a thing or matter.

word:greek-nt:G4492.explanation: Rhizoo means to cause to take root.

word:greek-nt:G4540.explanation: Samaria names a district and the city from which that district took its name.

word:greek-nt:G4579.explanation: Seio means to shake. It can also mean to agitate or stir up.

word:greek-nt:G4614.explanation: This word means “Sinai,” the proper name of a place mentioned in the New Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific place-name. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: twice in Acts and twice in Galatians. The name appears in Acts 7:30 and 7:38, and in Galatians 4:24–25. Its precise significance in each passage comes from the surrounding verse and argument, but the word itself consistently identifies Sinai.

word:greek-nt:G4661.explanation: This word refers to goods seized from a defeated person or enemy—“plunder” or “spoils.” It describes what is taken as the result of victory, rather than the act of fighting itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 11:22, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains the valuable possessions captured from someone who has been overcome.

word:greek-nt:G4823.explanation: Symbouleuō means to give advice or counsel. It can also describe people consulting together.

word:greek-nt:G4881.explanation: Synapollymi means to perish along with others.

word:greek-nt:G4988.explanation: Sosthenes is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, once in Acts and once in 1 Corinthians. The English Bible preserves it as “Sosthenes,” so the word functions as a name identifying an individual. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish additional details about his character, role, or relationship to others.

word:greek-nt:G5055.explanation: Teleō means to finish or bring something to completion. It can also mean to fulfill what has been written. It may describe accomplishing something. In another context, it means to pay.

word:greek-nt:G5107.explanation: Toiosde means such, or of this kind.

word:greek-nt:G5158.explanation: Tropos means a way or manner.

word:greek-nt:G5284.explanation: This word means “to sail the lee” or “to sail to the lee of”—to steer a vessel along the sheltered side of something, using its protection from the wind. It describes a specific sailing maneuver rather than sailing in general. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts 27, where the narrative describes sea travel. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object providing shelter.

word:greek-nt:G6018.explanation: This form means to ponder or think.
